This reflects the structural confounding from Section~\ref{sec:confounding}: single-facet corrections leave the uncorrected confound intact, producing invariant rank orderings (Observation~\ref{obs:ovb}). G-MFRM achieves $\tau = 0.857$ ($\rho = 0.952$), the only method to improve upon the baseline ranking ($\tau = 0.786$, $+$7.1pp). With $N = 8$ target models, the minimum detectable $\tau$ improvement is $2/\binom{8}{2} \approx 0.071$; the observed $\Delta\tau$ corresponds to a single pairwise swap, so the real-data result serves as illustrative evidence alongside the synthetic validation ($N = 50$, Section~\ref{sec:error_prop_results}). lines: A parallel line of work quantifies benchmark contamination at the item or model level without accounting for judge effects. ConStat \citep{constat2024} compares target model performance against a reference model to estimate contamination effects ($r^2 = 0.94$ with true contamination in controlled settings), establishing a principled quantification framework that G-MFRM's Stage~2 builds upon for exposure estimation. DCR \citep{dcr2025} adjusts scores on suspected leaked items through fuzzy inference rules, while LogProber \citep{logprober2024} detects memorization signatures from token-level log-probabilities under gray-box access. Perplexity-based methods such as Min-K\% \citep{mink2024} offer a simpler detection signal, but ConStat demonstrates that perplexity approaches are fundamentally evadable. All of these methods assume a fixed or averaged rater, so judge severity differences can masquerade as contamination signals. G-MFRM integrates contamination as a gated facet within the measurement model, separating both sources of distortion jointly rather than in sequence.

Rather than detecting or correcting for contamination post hoc, an alternative strategy prevents it by design. LiveBench \citep{livebench2025} constructs evaluation items from frequently updated sources (e.g., recent news, newly released datasets) so that items post-date model training cutoffs. TRUCE \citep{truce2024} keeps test sets private via confidential computing, evaluating models without revealing items to model owners. These approaches are complementary to G-MFRM: contamination avoidance reduces the prevalence of exposed items, while G-MFRM corrects for residual contamination on items that have already leaked.
